text: Binary search λ; check Σ(a − λb) ≥ 0.

0/1 fractional programming (0/1 分数规划): choose items (xi ∈ {0, 1}) to maximise Σ aixi / Σ bixi. Binary search the answer λ: the ratio can reach λ iff max Σ (ai − λ bi) xi ≥ 0. That check has no division, so it is an ordinary greedy / knapsack / shortest-path problem.

Why: Σa / Σb ≥ λ ⇔ Σa − λΣb ≥ 0 (with Σb > 0). The check is monotone in λ, so binary search works. Typical checks: "pick k items" (sort by a − λb), "weight at least W" (knapsack), "minimum mean cycle" (negative cycle with weights b·λ − a, 最小圈 P3199).

Talent Show (P4377): maximise talent / weight with total weight at least W; print ⌊1000 × ratio⌋. Weight states above W are merged into W, which is how "at least W" fits into a knapsack. Checked against trying every subset with exact fractions.
Iterate inside the j loop downward and read f[j] before it is changed in this item's pass: with the cap min(W, j + w), the target nj can equal j only when w = 0, which does not occur here.
f * g over divisors; Dirichlet prefix sums.

The Dirichlet convolution (狄利克雷卷积) of two arithmetic functions: (f * g)(n) = Σd | n f(d) g(n/d). Key identities, with 1(n) = 1, id(n) = n, ε(n) = [n = 1]: μ * 1 = ε (the μ property, 第9章), φ * 1 = id, μ * id = φ.
Multiplicative * multiplicative is multiplicative.
Dirichlet prefix sum (狄利克雷前缀和): b(n) = Σd | n a(d) for all n ≤ N in O(N log log N): for each prime p, for i = 1 … N/p add a[i] into a[i·p]. It is SOS DP (第12章) over the exponents of primes (P5495).

After processing prime p, a[n] holds the sum over divisors that differ from n only in the exponent of primes already processed, just like adding one bit at a time in SOS DP. Checked against summing all divisors directly in Python.
Increasing i inside one prime lets a value climb several powers of p (p, p², …) in the same pass, as required.
S(n) from H(n) and S(n/d); memo + small sieve.

Du's sieve (杜教筛) computes S(n) = Σi≤n f(i) for n up to about 2³¹, faster than sieving to n. Pick g so that h = f * g has an easy prefix sum. Then Σi≤n h(i) = Σd≤n g(d) S(⌊n/d⌋), and isolating d = 1: g(1)S(n) = H(n) − Σd=2..n g(d) S(⌊n/d⌋).

For φ choose g = 1 (φ * 1 = id, H(n) = n(n+1)/2); for μ choose g = 1 (μ * 1 = ε, H(n) = 1). Use division blocks for the sum, memoise S in a hash map, and sieve S directly for n up to about N2/3: total O(N2/3) (P4213).

Every n here is checked against a plain sieve in Python. The last one, 3·10⁶, is above the direct-sieve limit M = 2·10⁶, so it really goes through the recursion. The sum n(n+1)/2 still fits in long long for n < 2³¹.

title: 扩展中国剩余定理与威尔逊定理

text: Merging with gcd; (p − 1)! ≡ −1.

Extended CRT (扩展中国剩余定理): merge x ≡ r1 (mod m1) and x ≡ r2 (mod m2) when the moduli are not coprime. Write x = r1 + m1t; then m1t ≡ r2 − r1 (mod m2), a linear congruence (进阶篇第19章): solvable iff g = gcd(m1, m2) divides r2 − r1. The merged modulus is lcm(m1, m2).

Merge the equations one by one; products reach 10¹⁸, so multiply with __int128. Multi-variable linear Diophantine equations a1x1 + … + akxk = c are solvable iff gcd(a1, …, ak) | c; solve them by combining two coefficients at a time with exgcd.
x ≡ 5 (mod 6), x ≡ 3 (mod 10), x ≡ 2 (mod 9) with shared factors between moduli; checked by stepping in Python (P4777).
Return −1 as soon as one merge is impossible. Keep R reduced modulo the current M after every merge.

Wilson's theorem (威尔逊定理): p is prime ⇔ (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p). It is a characterisation, not a fast test, but it gives (p − 1)! mod p for free and helps simplify factorials modulo a prime, e.g. n! mod p with the multiples of p removed (used inside exLucas).
The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. Fractional: Σa/Σb ≥ λ ⇔ Σ(a − λb) ≥ 0; binary search λ.
2. Dirichlet: (f*g)(n) = Σ_{d|n} f(d)g(n/d); μ*1 = ε, φ*1 = id, μ*id = φ.
3. Dirichlet prefix: for each prime p, for i increasing: a[ip] += a[i].
4. Du: g(1)S(n) = H(n) − Σ_{d≥2} g(d)S(n/d); blocks + memo + sieve to N^(2/3).
5. exCRT: M t ≡ r − R (mod m), need gcd | diff; new modulus lcm.
6. Wilson: p prime ⇔ (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p).
